chapter_theme: The ascetics Civakan has argued with leave their households for the Jina, and he goes on to the Takka land and its city Kemamapuram, described as a goddess and a sea of wealth; there the merchant Subhadran's daughter Kemasari has waited twelve years under an astrologer's word that her husband is the man whose sight will shame her, while her father feeds a thousand and eight guests a day, and Civakan, meditating under a banyan outside the city, is met by the father, who begins to read his bodily marks.

cast.role: the hero, travelling alone toward the Takka land
the forest ascetics whose austerities Civakan answers and who turn to the Jina (called பாகத்தார் in 1437)
the merchant's daughter of Kemamapuram in the Takka land
the astrologer who reads Kemasari's birth and names the sign of her husband

1437.reading: Hearing what the hill-shouldered hero said, the ascetics of that side put away their households, saying that today their eyes had been opened, rose and went to the feet of the Conqueror and gained the good path of release; the sun went down and the noble one was rested.
1437.event: The forest ascetics, won over by Civakan's teaching, leave their families and take refuge with the Jina; night falls and Civakan rests.

claims.claim: one who takes refuge at the feet of the Jina gains the true path to release

1437.nuance: Their words (இன்று கண் விடுக்கப்பட்டேம்) treat the conversion as the opening of eyes, so their earlier austerities are cast as blindness. That they now leave their families (குடும்ப நீக்கி) answers the jibe of 1432 that these ascetics still lay with women in their leaf huts. பாகத்தார் is taken as 'those on that side', the ascetics.

1438.reading: Rested, at dawn when the darkness thinned, he learned the direction and the river from the blameless converts who showed him the way, and went on, he whose body bore the true marks, with none above him.
1438.event: At dawn the converted ascetics show Civakan the road, and he sets out.
1438.nuance: மெய்ப்பொறி யாக்கையான், the man whose body bears the true marks, anticipates the reading of his bodily marks that begins at 1460; the construal of மிசையும் இல்லது in line 4 is not sure.

1439.reading: He reached the border of the Takka land, a fitting country full of lotus ponds like a picture drawn on cloth, wide and sweet as the dark-gold skin of women with garlanded breasts.
1439.event: Civakan reaches the border of the Takka country.

1440.reading: The scent loosed from lotuses of the honeyed ponds, the sandal paste worn by flower-haired women and the fragrance of aghil smoke mingling everywhere make up the Takka land, they say.
1440.nuance: Line 4 is divided as printed (தாங்கலா றக்கநா டாய தென்பவே); the reading takes it as naming the Takka land through sandhi, but the first word is unclear.

1441.reading: Garlands of champak flowers, fragrant sandal, ripe areca with tender betel leaf, and food that fails no one: such is the look of that land of generous fame.

1442.reading: In the rich sugarcane-bordered fields the long red paddy lying across the lotuses at the bund looks like the forehead ornament of dancing women on the stage, with bees circling it.
1442.nuance: The simile turns on இலம்பகம, the frontlet worn on the brow, the same word that names the epic's books.

1443.reading: At the curving bee-haunted ghat the young vaalai fish, trembling as though a crab's claw had touched it, hides for shame and leaves its food; the poet turns to tell of the city ringed by a flowered moat fed by falling water.
1443.nuance: The fish that flees in shame is a playful prelude to the heroine, whose sign is to be shame at the sight of the man (1451).

1444.reading: The deep moat is the city goddess's silk, the snake-skin-smooth wall her famous girdle, the battlements her ornamented breasts, the gem-bright gate-tower her moon face, and the long flags her braided hair.

1445.reading: Since none who live there would leave it even if fed the nectar churned from the planted mountain, its shining golden wall is like a crest set upon the great city that holds heaped wealth.

1446.reading: With its flags held up like leaping sharks, mansions like mountains of rolling waves, great ships, women like the goddess Tiru and nectar, and its great roar, the rich city is a sounding sea, they say.

1447.reading: In every long street of mansions whose tops graze the moon, fallen opening garlands and dropped gold ornaments make it look like an opened treasure room, and it shines with a splendour strangers cannot walk through.

1448.reading: The golden city named Kemamapuram, of undying fame, is like a tilaka set on the earth, and its king, guardian of the land under a tall garlanded umbrella, is named Narapatidevan.

1449.reading: In that city lived a merchant like a king himself, matchless in person, bearing a well-made spear and fragrant garland, who passed his days beguiled by women with dark rain-cool eyes.
1449.nuance: வேத வாணிகன் in line 2 is unusual for a merchant; it may be a scribal form, and the reading keeps only 'merchant'.

1450.reading: Subhadran, of shoulders swelled by the bow and massed like hills, whose giving hand outdid the pouring cloud, had by his wife a daughter Kemasari, beyond all praise, who stood as the great lamp of womanhood whose fame was written in every direction.
1450.event: Kemasari is born to the merchant Subhadran and his wife.

1451.reading: On the day the stainless girl was born a man wise in reckoning worked it out by rule and said: the one at whose first sight she is suddenly overcome with shame will be her husband, so join them; and from that day the father keeps up a great feeding of guests.
1451.event: An astrologer foretells that Kemasari's husband will be the man whose sight makes her feel shame, and her father begins daily feasts for guests.
1451.nuance: The sign is the girl's own shame (நாண்), the virtue that normally keeps a maiden from a stranger's gaze; here it is made the test that marks the man. The feasting is the father's way of bringing men before her eyes.

1452.reading: Amid hanging garlands of gold, of broad flowers and of gems, the girl with bangled arms and waist a hand's span, shining like lightning, leans on a golden pillar and watches for the lover fate has appointed.
1452.event: Kemasari stands by a golden pillar watching the guests for her destined husband.
1452.nuance: ஊழ்படு காதலான் makes the husband a matter of ūḻ, apportioned before she sees him.

1453.reading: For the sake of the fortunate man who will be the bride's husband, a thousand and eight guests were fed each day with nectar-like rice in fitting ways, and so twelve years passed for that flower-creeper of a girl.
1453.event: For twelve years the household feeds a thousand and eight guests a day while Kemasari waits.

1454.reading: Seeing the beauty of the girl, her smiling red lips as if dyed with vermilion over the murukku petal, her full breasts, honeyed garland, curled hair and golden ornaments, her own mother cannot bear it, and melts and wastes.
1454.event: Kemasari's mother pines at seeing her daughter's beauty go unwed.

1455.reading: As her daughter's beauty, eyes like the tender mango, moon face and flowerlike grace, stayed alone and unused, the mother looked on like a doe struck by an arrow, her bangles slipping, and the garlanded father took away all her grief.

1456.reading: He says that as the spotted bee comes to a bud the moment its mouth opens, so the pleasure fit for women comes in its season; she need not grieve, for a man of full beauty, a lover great in merit, will meet the girl's eyes tomorrow.

claims.claim: a woman's joy in love comes at its own ripe time, as the bee comes to the opening bud

1456.nuance: தவத்தின் மிக்கான் is read as 'great by the merit of former austerity', the Jain way of naming the good fortune that brings a husband; the 'tomorrow' (நாளை) is borne out at once in 1457.

1457.reading: The prince with the warrior's anklet came near the town of the innocent wide-eyed girl, an unmatched flower creeper risen from golden ground, bright as lightning shot out, her hair braided like thick darkness.

1458.reading: The father of the young girl with jasmine-scented hair, a man of jewels spreading many-rayed light, came upon the prince at some distance from the fine city.
1458.event: Kemasari's father meets Civakan outside the city.
1458.nuance: சேட்பட் டானரோ is taken as சேண் படுதல், being far off; the line may instead mean that the father went out a long way to find him.

1459.reading: Like a fine red sun risen in the south and come round to the north, the man of the wedding-fit chest arrived and sat gladly in the shade of a banyan, meditating on the Lord.
1459.event: Civakan sits under a banyan tree in contemplation of the Jina.
1459.nuance: The hero on his way to a marriage he does not know of is shown at meditation, not seeking a bride, so the match comes to him as the prophecy's work rather than his pursuit.

1460.reading: His fine crowned head was like a spread umbrella, his two feet had the shape of a tortoise's back, his rounded flanks curved with the grace of a bow, and his eyes were the colour of the fragrant lotus.
1460.nuance: This opens a catalogue of auspicious bodily marks running to 1465, where the father reads them and decides that this is his daughter's husband; the marks are the second sign, beside the girl's shame.

links.note: In 1432 Civakan mocks the ascetics who leave soft beds only to lie with women in leaf huts; in 1437 they put away their households and go to the Jina.
links.teaches: The jibe was not only abuse but a charge the converts accept, so the poem counts their earlier forest life as no renunciation and their conversion as the first true leaving of home.

links.note: 1436 names knowledge, right faith and conduct whose fulness ends both kinds of deed; 1437 has the hearers rise and take the path of release.
links.teaches: The doctrine of the three jewels is tested at once by its hearers, and the epic settles the debate by conversion rather than by any further argument from the ascetics.

links.note: 1438 calls Civakan the man whose body bears the true marks; from 1460 the marks are listed one by one.
links.teaches: An epithet that seems mere praise on the road becomes the evidence by which a stranger is recognised as a destined husband, so the body itself carries the plot.

links.note: The astrologer foretells that Kemasari's husband is the man at whose sight she will feel sudden shame; in 1472 at first sight her restraint and shame give way and she melts.
links.teaches: The prophecy names shame as the sign, but its fulfilment is shame overwhelmed by desire, so the virtue that should guard a maiden is made the very place where the destined bond shows itself.

links.note: Both brides' fathers wait on an astrologer's word about the destined husband: Gandharvadattai's says he lives in Rajamapuram, Kemasari's that she will know him by her own shame.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two horoscopes show the epic varying one device: the Vidyadhara princess's husband is found by place and contest, the merchant's daughter's by a sign in her own body that no contest can stage.

links.note: The couplet praises the host who tends the departing guest and watches for the guest to come; Subhadran feeds a thousand and eight guests a day for twelve years watching for one guest who will be his son-in-law.
links.teaches: The epic takes the couplet's watching for the coming guest literally and turns it to a private end, so hospitality becomes a search, rewarded with a husband in this life rather than with welcome among the gods.

gains.a: the father's twelve-year feast is given the standing of a recognised householder's virtue rather than a mere device of the plot
gains.b: the couplet's 'watching for the guest to come' is shown to admit a host whose care has a hidden aim of his own, a case the couplet does not weigh

links.note: 1460 lists Civakan's bodily marks without saying who sees them; in 1465 the father, having examined them, decides he is his daughter's husband and takes him in his chariot.
links.teaches: The catalogue that reads as the poet's praise is revealed as a merchant's inspection, so the marks of a great man work as a test of a bridegroom alongside the astrologer's sign.

new_concepts.gloss: an omen or sign read as foretelling what will come
new_concepts.label_source: label from 1129; here the astrologer's reckoning (விதியின் எண்ணி, 1451) and the bodily marks (மெய்ப்பொறி, 1438)

source_issues: 1437, 1447, 1450, 1451, 1454 and 1456 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build.
1440 line 4 (தாங்கலா றக்கநா டாய தென்பவே) is divided obscurely; the first word cannot be fixed.
1449 line 2 has வேத வாணிகன், an unusual title for the merchant; perhaps a scribal form.
1458 line 3 (சேட்பட் டானரோ) is obscure as divided.
1444 line 2 has நாயில் for ஞாயில் (battlements), a variant spelling.
